**Two Minute Hands**

On the front of the Corn Exchange in Bristol there is a clock with two minute hands. They sit a little over ten minutes apart and sweep around the dial together, never catching each other. One shows London time. The other shows Bristol time, which was once a real and separate thing.

Bristol is about two and a half degrees west of London, so the sun reaches its highest point there roughly ten minutes later. For most of history, that was simply what time meant. Noon was the moment the sun stood highest over the place where you were standing. Every town kept its own noon, set its church clock by it, and was correct. A traveler going west by coach would find their watch drifting ahead of the local clocks, but coaches were slow enough that nobody much cared. You reset your watch when you arrived, the same way you'd adjust to the local accent.

The railway broke this. A train timetable is a promise about when a machine will be in a particular place, and that promise is hard to keep when every station along the line disagrees about what time it is. The Great Western Railway started running its trains on London time in 1840, and other companies followed. For several decades after, many British towns lived with two times at once: the railway's and their own. Some put up clocks like Bristol's. Some simply refused, and kept local time on the town hall as a matter of pride. Britain didn't make Greenwich time the legal standard until 1880, forty years after the trains had made it the practical one.

The American version was messier, because the country was wider. By the early 1880s, railroads in the United States were operating on dozens of different times, each company keeping the time of its headquarters city. A station served by several lines might display a clock for each. Then, on November 18, 1883, the railroads switched to a system of four zones, all at once, by private agreement. No law required it. Congress didn't get around to making standard time official until 1918. In cities on the eastern side of each new zone, clocks were stopped and set back partway through the day, so the sun crossed overhead and then the clocks struck twelve a second time. People called it the day of two noons.

What I like about this story is how much grumbling there was, and how reasonable the grumbling sounds in retrospect. People understood that something was being taken from them. Their noon, which had been a fact about the sky, was being replaced with a noon that was a fact about a railroad company's convenience. Some newspapers and preachers complained that railroad time was displacing the time God had provided. Detroit kept arguing about which time to use well into the twentieth century. These people lost, and it's good that they lost, but they weren't confused about what was happening. Time was being converted from an observation into an agreement.

The agreement has always shown its seams, and they are political all the way down. When an international conference in 1884 chose Greenwich as the world's prime meridian, France abstained and kept using Paris time for another 27 years. When France finally gave in, the law defined French time as Paris mean time delayed by nine minutes and twenty-one seconds, which is Greenwich time, phrased so that the word "Greenwich" never had to appear.

The seams are still visible today. Spain sits at roughly the same longitude as Britain but keeps the same time as Germany, because Franco moved the clocks in 1940 and nobody moved them back. This is part of why Spaniards seem to eat dinner so late. By the sun, they're eating at a fairly ordinary hour. China spans enough longitude for five time zones and uses one, so in the far west the sun can rise at ten in the morning by the official clock, and many people in Xinjiang informally keep a second time two hours behind Beijing. Nepal is offset from its neighbors by fifteen minutes, at UTC+5:45, a small declaration that it is not India. Each of these is a decision someone made, for reasons that had little to do with the sun.

I think about this sometimes because it's such a clean example of a thing that feels natural and isn't. If you ask someone what time it is, they'll glance at a phone and tell you, with the same confidence they'd have reporting the temperature. But the temperature is a measurement, while the time is closer to a treaty. It's the output of a long chain of committees, railway managers, legislators, and, these days, a network of atomic clocks whose readings are averaged together by an office outside Paris. Even the length of the day is negotiated. The earth's rotation is slightly irregular, so for decades timekeepers have inserted occasional leap seconds to keep clocks in line with the planet. In 2022 the people in charge of such things voted to stop doing that by 2035, because leap seconds cause trouble for computers. When that happens, clock time will drift away from the sun, slowly, by design. The last thread connecting our noon to the actual sky will be allowed to go slack.

I don't think this is a tragedy. Standard time is one of the great quiet achievements of coordination, and nearly everything about modern life depends on it. But I find it worth remembering that it was an invention and a fairly recent one. It replaced something that worked perfectly well for people whose lives happened within a day's walk. A sundial in Bristol still tells the truth about Bristol. It just isn't the truth anyone needs anymore.

The second minute hand on the Corn Exchange clock has had no practical use for well over a century. Nobody in Bristol catches a train by it or opens a shop by it. The city keeps it running anyway, ten minutes behind, pointing at a noon that used to belong to the town.
